title: Build a Web Scraper in Go

lessons.title: Welcome
lessons.readme:
# Welcome

In this project, we'll build a [Web Crawler](https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/bots/what-is-a-web-crawler/) in Golang! To rank well in Google Search, websites need to [internally link pages one to another](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2008/10/importance-of-link-architecture). For example, a blog post about the _benefits_ of haircuts should probably link to my post about the best places to _get_ haircuts.

We're going to write a Golang [CLI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Command-line_interface) application that generates an "internal links" report for any website on the internet by crawling each page of the site.

## [!windows] for Windows Users

> [!warning]
> If you try to complete this course without [WSL 2](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install) installed on Windows, you're gonna have a bad time.

## Learning Goals

- Get hands-on practice with local Go development and tooling
- Practice making HTTP requests in Go
- Learn how to parse HTML with Golang
- Practice unit testing

## Setup

Before we dive into the project, let's make sure you are all set up properly. You will need:

1. The latest [Go toolchain](https://go.dev/doc/install) installed.
2. If you're using VS Code, I recommend installing the [Go extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=golang.Go). It's not required, but it makes working with Go a lot easier.
3. You will need the [Boot.dev CLI](https://github.com/bootdotdev/bootdev#bootdev-cli) installed, and you'll need to be [logged in](https://github.com/bootdotdev/bootdev?tab=readme-ov-file#usage).

## Assignment

Type `go version` to make sure that you have Go installed.

**Submit** the CLI tests. There's no penalty on failure for this lesson.

lessons.title: Golang Setup
lessons.readme:
# Golang Setup

Let's just get our Go project set up and running. We'll start with a simple "Hello, World!" program.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Create a new `main.go` file in your project root. It should be part of `package main`. Add a `main` function that simply prints `"Hello, World!"` to the console.
2. [ ] [Create a Go module](https://golang.org/doc/tutorial/create-module) in the root of your project. Here's the command:

```bash
go mod init MODULE_NAME
```

I recommend naming the module by its remote Git location (you should store all your projects in Git!). For example, my GitHub name is `wagslane` so my module name might be `github.com/wagslane/crawler`.

3. [ ] Build your program:

```bash
go build -o crawler
```

4. [ ] Run your program:

```bash
./crawler
```

You should see `"Hello, World!"` printed to the console.

5. [ ] Add a [.gitignore](https://git-scm.com/docs/gitignore) file to your project root and have Git ignore the `crawler` binary file.

**Submit** the CLI tests from **your project's root**. There's no penalty on failure for this lesson.

## Tip

Using `go build` and `./crawler` is a bit cumbersome. Building is best for production code, because it means the person running your program doesn't need to have Go installed.

However, for development, you can use `go run .` to compile and run your program in one step.

# Extract Page Content Our web crawler will need to know how to read a page of [HTML](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn/Getting_started_with_the_web/HTML_basics). Now that we can normalize URLs, let's start extracting actual content from web pages. A web scraper that only normalizes URLs isn't very useful - we need to parse HTML and extract the meaningful information. Let's start with just parsing the `

` and first `

` tags. For example, from this HTML page: ```html

Welcome to Boot.dev

Learn to code by building real projects.

This is the second paragraph.

``` We want to extract: - `

`: "Welcome to Boot.dev" - The first `

`: "Learn to code by building real projects." ## Assignment 1. [ ] Write tests for a new function called `getHeadingFromHTML`. Here's the signature: ```go func getHeadingFromHTML(html string) string ``` - `html` is an HTML string - In your tests make sure that the function returns the text content of the `

` tag if present, or the `

` tag as a fallback. - Returns an empty string if neither an `

` nor an `

` tag is found. 2. [ ] Implement the `getHeadingFromHTML` function. We'll be using the [`goquery`](https://github.com/PuerkitoBio/goquery) library. Install the dependency first: ```bash go get github.com/PuerkitoBio/goquery ``` I'll try not to give too many hints: read the package [docs](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/PuerkitoBio/goquery) for references. Reading docs is vital practice, that said, here are a few hints: - [`.Find()`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/PuerkitoBio/goquery#Selection.Find) scans the document looking for the passed in tag. Check the returned type. - The `goquery.NewDocumentFromReader` expects an `io.Reader` type to read data from. You can use `strings.NewReader(html)` to satisfy that. 3. [ ] Write a new function called `getFirstParagraphFromHTML` and some tests. Here's the signature: ```go func getFirstParagraphFromHTML(html string) string ``` - In your tests make sure that the tests return the text content of the _first_ `

` tag. - Returns an empty string if no `

` tag is found. > [!tip] > You may find that the first `

` tag doesn't always have the best or most useful results. I'd recommend searching for the `

` tag if it exists and find the first `

` tag within it, if it doesn't exist fallback to just > the first `

` tag. Here are some example test cases to get you started: ```go func TestGetHeadingFromHTMLBasic(t *testing.T) { inputBody := "

Test Title

" actual := getHeadingFromHTML(inputBody) expected := "Test Title" if actual != expected { t.Errorf("expected %q, got %q", expected, actual) } } func TestGetFirstParagraphFromHTMLMainPriority(t *testing.T) { inputBody := `

Outside paragraph.

Main paragraph.

` actual := getFirstParagraphFromHTML(inputBody) expected := "Main paragraph." if actual != expected { t.Errorf("expected %q, got %q", expected, actual) } } ``` 4. [ ] Make sure you have at least 3 test cases for each function you are testing! **Run and submit** the CLI tests from the **root of your module**.

lessons.title: Extract Links and Images
lessons.readme: # Extract Links and Images We need to extract links from the HTML both the links people can click AND the images that are displayed. This gives us a complete picture of what resources each page references. For example, this HTML page has both a link and an image: ```html Go to Boot.dev ``` We need to extract both `https://crawler-test.com` (from the link) and `/logo.png` (from the image). ## Assignment 1. [ ] Write tests for a new function called `getURLsFromHTML`. Here's the signature: ```go func getURLsFromHTML(htmlBody string, baseURL *url.URL) ([]string, error) { ``` - `htmlBody` is an HTML string - `baseURL` is the (already parsed) _root_ URL of the website we're crawling. This will allow us to rewrite [relative URLs into absolute URLs](https://www.seoclarity.net/resources/knowledgebase/difference-relative-absolute-url-15325/). - It returns an _un-normalized_ list of all the URLs found within the HTML, and an error if one occurs. In your tests, make sure that: - relative URLs are converted to absolute URLs - you find _all_ the `` tags in a body of HTML Here's one example test case to give you an idea: ```go func TestGetURLsFromHTMLAbsolute(t *testing.T) { inputURL := "https://crawler-test.com" inputBody := `Boot.dev` baseURL, err := url.Parse(inputURL) if err != nil { t.Errorf("couldn't parse input URL: %v", err) return } actual, err := getURLsFromHTML(inputBody, baseURL) if err != nil { t.Fatalf("unexpected error: %v", err) } expected := []string{"https://crawler-test.com"} if !reflect.DeepEqual(actual, expected) { t.Errorf("expected %v, got %v", expected, actual) } } ``` 2. [ ] Implement the `getURLsFromHTML` function. Continue using the [`goquery`](https://github.com/PuerkitoBio/goquery) library. Here are a few hints you may find useful: - The [Find](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/PuerkitoBio/goquery#Selection.Find) method returns a [Selection](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/PuerkitoBio/goquery#Selection) type. That type has a lot of helper methods. Take a look at the [Each](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/PuerkitoBio/goquery#Selection.Each) method. That's an iterator that will help you check the matching elements. For example: ```go doc.Find("a[href]").Each(func(_ int, s *goquery.Selection) { // For each '' it finds, it will run this function. }) ``` - In HTML, "anchor" elements are links with their `href` attribute containing the actual URL. e.g: ```html Learn Backend Development ``` 3. [ ] Write tests for a new function called `getImagesFromHTML`. Here's the signature: ```go func getImagesFromHTML(htmlBody string, baseURL *url.URL) ([]string, error) { ``` - `htmlBody` is an HTML string - `baseURL` is the (already parsed) _root_ URL of the website we're crawling. This will allow us to rewrite [relative URLs into absolute URLs](https://www.seoclarity.net/resources/knowledgebase/difference-relative-absolute-url-15325/). - It returns an _un-normalized_ list of all the image URLs found within the HTML, and an error if one occurs. In your tests, make sure: - relative URLs are converted to absolute URLs - Handle cases where attributes might be missing Here's one example test case to give you an idea: ```go func TestGetImagesFromHTMLRelative(t *testing.T) { inputURL := "https://crawler-test.com" inputBody := `` baseURL, err := url.Parse(inputURL) if err != nil { t.Errorf("couldn't parse input URL: %v", err) return } actual, err := getImagesFromHTML(inputBody, baseURL) if err != nil { t.Fatalf("unexpected error: %v", err) } expected := []string{"https://crawler-test.com/logo.png"} if !reflect.DeepEqual(actual, expected) { t.Errorf("expected %v, got %v", expected, actual) } } ``` 4. [ ] Implement the `getImagesFromHTML` function. 5. [ ] Make sure you have at least 3 test cases for each function you're testing. **Run and submit** the CLI tests from the **root of your module**.

# Structure Page Data So far we've built functions to help us normalize URLs and extract links/text from HTML. Now let's structure that data in a way that's much more usable. ## Assignment 1. [ ] Write tests for a new function called `extractPageData`. Here's the signature: ```go func extractPageData(html, pageURL string) PageData { ``` - `html` is an HTML string - `pageURL` is the absolute URL of the page (used for converting relative URLs) - It returns a struct with fields: `URL`, `Heading`, `FirstParagraph`, `OutgoingLinks`, `ImageURLs` Here's one example test case to get you started: ```go func TestExtractPageData(t *testing.T) { inputURL := "https://crawler-test.com" inputBody := `

Test Title

This is the first paragraph.

Link 1 ` actual := extractPageData(inputBody, inputURL) expected := PageData{ URL: "https://crawler-test.com", Heading: "Test Title", FirstParagraph: "This is the first paragraph.", OutgoingLinks: []string{"https://crawler-test.com/link1"}, ImageURLs: []string{"https://crawler-test.com/image1.jpg"}, } if !reflect.DeepEqual(actual, expected) { t.Errorf("expected %+v, got %+v", expected, actual) } } ``` 2. [ ] Implement the `extractPageData` function. _You have already built all the logic for this function_, it just needs to return the data you're already gathering in a struct! **Run and submit** the CLI tests to verify your extraction logic works correctly!

lessons.title: Main
lessons.readme:
# Main

Let's get to work on the actual application! Our program takes as a [command line argument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Command-line_interface#Arguments) the website URL we want to crawl (or at least the page we want to start from).

```bash
go build -o crawler && ./crawler BASE_URL
```

Or

```bash
go run . BASE_URL
```

Where `BASE_URL` is the root URL of the website we want to crawl. For example: `https://learnwebscraping.dev/practice/ecommerce/`.

You will need to [process command line arguments](https://gobyexample.com/command-line-arguments) for this step.

All your main function should do at this point is:

1. [ ] If the number of CLI arguments is less than 1, print "no website provided" and exit with code 1.
2. [ ] If the number of CLI arguments is more than 1, print "too many arguments provided" and exit with code 1.
3. [ ] If we have exactly one CLI argument, it's the `BASE_URL`, so print a message letting the user know the crawler is starting at that URL: `starting crawl of: BASE_URL`, where `BASE_URL` is the URL provided as the CLI argument.

## Test by Running

This is a good example of some code that's a bit weird to test with unit tests. Just run the dang thing with too few, just the right amount, and too many arguments to ensure it behaves as expected.

**Run and submit** the CLI tests from the **root of your `main` package**.

## Tips

- I used [os.Exit](https://golang.org/pkg/os/#Exit) to exit the program with a status code of 1. This is a good way to signal to the operating system that something went wrong.
- `os.Args` holds the CLI arguments, with the first item as the program path and the rest being the actual arguments, `os.Args[1:]`.

lessons.title: Get HTML
lessons.readme:
# Get HTML

Let's start crawling real web pages! For these remaining steps, use `https://learnwebscraping.dev/practice/ecommerce/`. A single product page like `https://learnwebscraping.dev/practice/ecommerce/products/ashenfang-longsword-fan-1001/` is a good place to start.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Create a `getHTML` function that takes a URL string and returns an HTML string and error.

```go
func getHTML(rawURL string) (string, error)
```

For now, your function should:

1. [ ] Use [http.NewRequest](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#NewRequest) with an [http.Client](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#Client) to fetch the webpage of the `rawURL`. Set a `User-Agent` header (e.g. `BootCrawler/1.0`) to avoid being blocked by servers.
2. [ ] Return an error if the [HTTP status code](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status) is an error-level code (400+)
3. [ ] Return an error if the response [`content-type` header](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Type) is not `text/html`
4. [ ] Return any other possible errors
5. [ ] Return the webpage's HTML if successful

> [!tip]
> You may find [`io.ReadAll`](https://pkg.go.dev/io#ReadAll) helpful in reading the response.

I'd argue that it's **not necessary to create unit tests** for a function like `getHTML`. It's primarily just side effects (internet access), making it _not_ a pure function like `normalizeURL` and `getURLsFromHTML`. Most of the "logic" in `getHTML` is just a couple of standard library function calls: and there's not much reason to test the standard library.

6. [ ] Call `getHTML` from your `main` function and print the result. It should print some HTML that it fetched from the internet!

**Run and submit** the CLI tests.

Notice that they're grabbing some HTML from the main page of Wikipedia.

lessons.title: Adding Recursion
lessons.readme:
# Adding Recursion

This is going to be the largest step so far, and will require the most "figuring it out on your own"... **you got this**.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Create a `crawlPage` function that [uses recursion](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recursion_(computer_science)>) to traverse a website. Recursion is useful because we want to continue to crawl each URL we find on a page until we've crawled every page on the site. Here's my function signature:

```go
func crawlPage(rawBaseURL, rawCurrentURL string, pages map[string]int)
```

- `rawCurrentURL` is the _current_ URL we're crawling
- `rawBaseURL` is the _root_ URL of the website we're crawling

In the first call to `crawlPage()` `rawCurrentURL` is a copy of `rawBaseURL`, but as we make further HTTP requests to all the URLs we find on the `rawBaseURL`, the `rawCurrentURL` value will change while the base stays the same.

The `pages` map keeps track of the number of times we've seen each internal link. This function should continue to pass the same map to itself.

Here's my pseudocode:

- Make sure the `rawCurrentURL` is on the same domain as the `rawBaseURL`. If it's not, just `return`. We don't want to crawl the entire internet, just the domain in question.
- Get a normalized version of the `rawCurrentURL`.
- If the `pages` map already has an entry for the normalized version of the current URL, just increment the count and be done, we've already crawled this page.
- Otherwise, add an entry to the `pages` map for the normalized version of the current URL, and set the count to `1`.
- Get the HTML from the current URL, and add a print statement so you can watch your crawler in real-time.
- Assuming all went well with the request, get all the URLs from the response body HTML
- Recursively crawl each URL on the page

> [!danger]
> Be careful testing this! Be sure to add print statements so you can see what your crawler is doing, and **kill it with [[Ctrl]]+[[C]] if it's stuck in a loop**. If you make too many spammy requests to a website (including the sandbox) you could get your IP address blocked.

2. [ ] Call `crawlPage` in the `main` function instead of `getHTML`. When it's complete, print the keys and values of the `pages` map to the console.
3. [ ] Test your program by running it against `https://learnwebscraping.dev/practice/ecommerce/`.

```sh
go run . https://learnwebscraping.dev/practice/ecommerce/
```

4. [ ] When you're satisfied that everything is working, you can move on.

lessons.title: Concurrency
lessons.readme:
# Concurrency

Why write a web crawler with Go and not use concurrency? Let's speed this bad boy up with some goroutines!

To coordinate the goroutines, we'll use:

- A [Mutex](https://pkg.go.dev/sync#Mutex) to protect the shared `pages` map.
- A [buffered channel](https://go.dev/tour/concurrency/3) of empty structs to limit concurrent requests. Each request sends a token when it starts and receives one when it finishes. Sends block when the buffer is full.
- A [WaitGroup](https://pkg.go.dev/sync#WaitGroup) to keep `main` from exiting until all requests finish.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Create a [struct](https://tour.golang.org/moretypes/2) to share the `pages` map, base URL, and synchronization primitives between goroutines. Here's an example of what I used:
   ```go
   type config struct {
       pages              map[string]PageData
       baseURL            *url.URL
       mu                 *sync.Mutex
       concurrencyControl chan struct{}
       wg                 *sync.WaitGroup
   }
   ```
2. [ ] Update `crawlPage` to use the shared struct and store page data instead of counts:

   ```go
   func (cfg *config) crawlPage(rawCurrentURL string)
   ```

   - Fetch each normalized URL at most once, even when multiple goroutines discover it.
   - Store the result of `extractPageData` for each successfully fetched page, using the current page's URL, and crawl its `OutgoingLinks`.
   - Keep access to the shared `pages` map safe with the mutex.

3. [ ] Update `main` to initialize the shared struct and print discovered URLs instead of counts.
4. [ ] **Test it (I tested it manually again).** I recommend setting your `maxConcurrency` (the buffer size of the `concurrencyControl` channel) to 1 to start to just make sure everything still works. Then bump it up to 2. Make sure it still works, and that it's about twice as fast. Then bump it up to 5 or 10. Make sure you still get the same data, but it should be _much_ faster.

When you're satisfied with the results, you can move on.

## Tips

I created this method to call as a helper inside of `crawlPage`:

```go
func (cfg *config) addPageVisit(normalizedURL string) (shouldVisit bool)
```

- Make sure you're _not_ crawling the same page multiple times. That's why my `addPageVisit` method returns a boolean: to indicate whether we should crawl the page.
- I [defer](https://tour.golang.org/flowcontrol/12) a [wg.Done()](https://pkg.go.dev/sync#WaitGroup.Done) and a receive from the (`<-cfg.concurrencyControl`) channel. This ensures that the `wg` is decremented and the channel is emptied even when the goroutine errors and returns early.
- Make sure you [wg.Add](https://pkg.go.dev/sync#WaitGroup.Add) _before_ you spawn a goroutine, but that you send into the channel _after but still at the start_ of a new goroutine.
- Because all the recursive calls share a wait group, you should only need to [wg.Wait()](https://pkg.go.dev/sync#WaitGroup.Wait) once in the `main` function.

lessons.title: Max Pages
lessons.readme:
# Max Pages

As it stands, our crawler is only useful on fairly small sites. Sites with thousands or _hundreds of thousands_ of pages take too long to crawl.

_Google's crawlers run concurrently on fleets of servers to crawl the majority of the internet. You might not have that kind of budget for this project._

Let's add a `maxPages` setting so that we can crawl even gigantic websites and have our tool automatically stop when it's done a reasonable amount of work.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Add a `maxPages` integer to your `config` struct. This will be the maximum number of pages to crawl.
2. [ ] Update your `crawlPage` function to return immediately at the start of the function if the length of the `pages` map is greater than or equal to `maxPages`. _Make sure you safely access the `pages` map with the mutex!_
3. [ ] Make both the `maxConcurrency` and `maxPages` settings configurable via command-line args.
4. [ ] Now you should be able to run your program with this syntax:

```bash
go build -o crawler

# usage: ./crawler URL maxConcurrency maxPages
./crawler "https://learnwebscraping.dev/practice/ecommerce/" 3 10
```

_`go build` and `./crawler` can also be replaced with `go run .` from your `main` package directory._

Make sure that your program prints a line to the console each time you crawl a page, as well as once per page in the report. This will help you see what your crawler is doing, and ensure you can kill it with [[Ctrl]]+[[C]] if it's stuck in a loop or spamming requests.

**Run and submit** the CLI tests.

lessons.title: JSON Report
lessons.readme:
# JSON Report

We're almost done! Our web crawler now extracts rich data from every page and stores it efficiently in a map. Let's export it to JSON so it's easy to read and share.

For example, one page record in that map might look like this:

```go
pages := map[string]PageData{
    "learnwebscraping.dev/practice/ecommerce/products/ashenfang-longsword-fan-1001": {
        URL:            "https://learnwebscraping.dev/practice/ecommerce/products/ashenfang-longsword-fan-1001/",
        Heading:        "Ashenfang Longsword",
        FirstParagraph: "A balanced battlefield blade with a smoldering fuller and leather-wrapped grip.",
        OutgoingLinks: []string{
            "https://learnwebscraping.dev/practice/ecommerce/",
            "https://learnwebscraping.dev/practice/ecommerce/categories/",
            "https://learnwebscraping.dev/practice/ecommerce/categories/longswords/",
        },
        ImageURLs: []string{"https://learnwebscraping.dev/images/catalog/longswords.svg"},
    },
}
```

We want to create a `report.json` file containing a sorted array of all page records.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Add JSON struct tags to `PageData` in `extract_page_data.go`:

```go
type PageData struct {
    URL            string   `json:"url"`
    Heading        string   `json:"heading"`
    FirstParagraph string   `json:"first_paragraph"`
    OutgoingLinks  []string `json:"outgoing_links"`
    ImageURLs      []string `json:"image_urls"`
}
```

2. [ ] Create a new file called `json_report.go`.
3. [ ] Import Go's built-in [`encoding/json` package](https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json):

```go
import "encoding/json"
```

4. [ ] Create a new function called `writeJSONReport`. Here's the signature:

```go
func writeJSONReport(pages map[string]PageData, filename string) error
```

5. [ ] Implement `writeJSONReport`. It should:
   - Sort the map keys for deterministic output
   - Build a `[]PageData` slice in sorted order
   - Marshal it with [`json.MarshalIndent`](https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json#MarshalIndent) using `indent=2`
   - Write the result to disk with [`os.WriteFile`](https://pkg.go.dev/os#WriteFile)

Here are some tips:

- Sort keys: `sort.Strings(keys)`
- Marshal: `data, err := json.MarshalIndent(sorted, "", "  ")`
- Write: `os.WriteFile(filename, data, 0644)`

6. [ ] Update your `main.go` to use the JSON report:
   - Call `writeJSONReport(cfg.pages, "report.json")` after crawling completes

7. [ ] Test your implementation:
   - Verify `report.json` is created after running the crawler
   - Check that it contains a valid JSON array of page objects

**Run and submit** the CLI tests.

lessons.title: Submit the Link to Your Repository!
lessons.readme:
# Submit the Link to Your Repository!

If you haven't been keeping track of your project in Git, you should be! Once you have your finished project in a public Git repository, submit the link to your project in the text box to the right! Submit a public HTTPS Git clone URL, for example: `https://github.com/github-username/repo-name`.

I hope you've enjoyed the project, it's always good to solidify the things you learn in courses by getting your hands dirty with a real project.

## Ideas for Extending the Project

- Make the script run on a timer and deploy it to a server. Have it email you every so often with a report.
- Add more robust error checking so that you can crawl larger sites without issues.
- Count external links, as well as internal links, and add them to the report
- Use a graphics library to create an image that shows the links between the pages as a graph visualization
- Make requests concurrently to speed up the crawling process
- Add a `README.md` file explaining to users how to clone your git repo and get started
